background.definition: Human scabies is a contagious infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei.

list.listitem: 3.5/1000/year males.
4.4/1000/year females.
Estimated global prevalence of 300 million cases.
Accounts for 0.07% global burden of disease measured in disability adjusted life years.
COVID-19 pandemic and migration are contributing to an increased incidence of scabies.
Sarcoptes scabiei var hominis, which belongs to the class Arachnida.
The mite can survive outside the host for 2 to 3 days. It burrows under the corneal layer of the epidermis, where it feeds and lays its ova.
Incubation times vary from 15 to 20 days (average), or up to 6 weeks.
Common infestations consist of 10 to 20 parasites per individual.
After 10 days to 4 weeks, and with subsequent infections, a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to the mites, eggs, and feces occurs.
In crusted, or Norwegian, scabies there may be hundreds to millions of mites that infect an immunodeficient or debilitated individual.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Prolonged body contact with infected individual

Differential.Differential_Features: Typical distribution, chronic course, family history of atopy
Localized bullae and erosions with honey-colored crust, no diffuse pruritus
Vesico-pustular recurrent rash on the hands, wrists, feet, and ankles; rare after the age of 2
History of bites; if fleas, the lesions are often on the lower legs only and may be urticarial
Groups of vesicles on extensor surfaces, positive IgA immunofluorescence on skin biopsy; rare

list.listitem: Consider scabies in patients with generalized itch that is worse at night and the presence of papules, vesicles, or burrows in the typical predilection sites which include the fingerwebs and sides, wrists, axillae, areolae and genital area; also consider scabies in household members or contacts with itch.
Nodules around the axillae or navel or on the penis or scrotum are pathognomonic.

The combination of diffuse itching with visible lesions, with either at least 2 typical locations of scabies, or presence of a household member with itch, was 100% sensitive and 97% specific in a high prevalence population in Africa.
A positive skin scraping for mites, eggs, fecal pellets, or fragments is specific for the confirmed diagnosis of scabies.
A negative skin scraping does not rule out the diagnosis.

Guidelines define confirmed scabies as requiring visualization of one of mite, eggs, or feces from a skin sample. Clinical scabies is defined as at least one of scabies burrows, typical lesions affecting male genitalia , or typical lesions in a typical distribution.
Dermoscopy may be helpful as a noninvasive diagnostic test. It can be used to look for the arrowhead sign. This is a mite that looks like a small arrowhead at the end of a burrow.
However, no robust studies have been done comparing the sensitivity and specificity of clinical diagnosis and microscopic examinations of the skin.
Consider scabies in patients with generalized itch that is worse at night, with papules, vesicles, or burrows in the typical predilection sites and household members or contacts with itch.
Skin scraping can confirm the diagnosis, but a negative scraping does not exclude it. Dermoscopy may be helpful.
Initial therapy should be topical permethrin for most patients.
Topical permethrin, topical ivermectin, and oral ivermectin appear equally effective and safe in the treatment of scabies. A

Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg orally is another effective treatment for uncomplicated scabies and cases that are resistant to initial treatment. The dose may be repeated in 1 to 2 weeks if needed. A
Alternative treatments to consider when permethrin is not available include malathion, sulfur, natural pyrethrins, A and topical 25% benzyl benzoate. B

Permethrin 5% cream is the recommended initial treatment for scabies in all persons, including infants 2 months and older, children, pregnant, and lactating women. Apply to all areas of the body from the neck down overnight and wash off after 8 to 14 hours. Apply to the hairline, neck, scalp, temple and forehead in infants and elderly. It may be repeated in 2 weeks if needed.

Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg is another effective treatment for scabies. Some experts recommend repeating the dose in 1 to 2 weeks. One RCT showed that 2 doses of ivermectin is as effective as a single application of permethrin.
However, a Cochrane review in 2018 found comparable efficacy between one to three applications of topical permethrin and one to three doses of oral ivermectin.

A prospective, double-blind RCT showed comparable benefit between a single application of 5% permethrin, single dose (200 mcg/kg orally) ivermectin, and double dose ivermectin (repeated after 2 weeks). The topical treatment showed faster improvement at the first week follow up.
A population based non-randomized controlled trial showed ivermectin en masse was highly effective for a population with endemic scabies and significantly more effective than topical permethrin.
Alternative treatments to consider when permethrin, a synthetic pyrethroid, is not available include topical benzyl benzoate, malathion, topical sulfur ointment,and natural pyrethrins.

A double-blinded RCT enrolling 110 patients 12 years and older from a single institution in Austria found topical benzyl benzoate 25% applied daily for 3 days to be significantly more effective than permethrin 5% applied daily for 3 days for treating scabies at 3 to 4 weeks post treatment (87% vs 27%; P<.001; NNT = 2). Mild to moderate adverse events, like burning or stinging, were higher with benzyl benzoate than permethrin (43% vs 6%; P<.001; NNTH = 3), but they were transient and cleared spontaneously. Benzyl benzoate is not expensive and is easy to find over the counter.

Lindane can cause neurotoxicity, particularly when used more often than the manufacturers recommend or applied to broken skin. A nonblinded RCT showed superiority of ivermectin over lindane, although there was a higher dropout rate at 4 weeks for ivermectin.

No controlled studies have been conducted for crusted or Norwegian scabies. Options include 1 to 2 or more doses of ivermectin 200 mcg/kg, at 2-weekly intervals, with or without weekly application of permethrin 5% cream, and daily keratolytics until all crusts are gone.

Topical spinosad 0.9% in a single application was shown in two vehicle controlled trials with 551 patients to be more effective than vehicle (78% vs 40%, p < 0.001, NNT = 3). It was well tolerated with few adverse effects.
Oral anti-histamines, emollients, and mild topical corticosteroids can help with post-treatment itching.

A network meta-analysis of 52 RCTs showed that combination permethrin plus oral ivermectin had a non-significantly higher cure rate than permethrin. In addition, combination permethrin plus oral ivermectin was ranked highest in terms of cure rate, topical ivermectin highest in terms of lowest chance of persistent itching, and pyrethrins highest in terms of lowest risk of adverse events.
In vitro studies have shown effectiveness of tea tree oil against mites.
A single blinded clinical trial in Nigeria showed effectiveness of bush tea essential oil compared with benzyl benzoate.
A pilot study in India showed that a paste with extracts of neem and turmeric cured 97% patients with scabies.
Treat all members in the same household, not just those with symptoms.
Wash clothing and bedding in hot water (>50°C).
Consider screening for other STI.
The duration of therapy is 1 to 2 weeks.
Consider referring patients with resistant or recurrent scabies to a dermatologist.
Treat bacterial superinfection with appropriate antibiotics.
The disease does not resolve spontaneously and untreated can lead to secondary infection, dermatitis, and development of the crusted form. C
The rash and pruritus of scabies might persist for up to 2 weeks after treatment. C
Itching can be improved with antihistamines; consider non sedating antihistamines during the daytime and sedating antihistamines at night. C

Clinical cure cannot be considered definitive until about 28 days after treatment, when all lesions present at the time of treatment should either be healed or resolving, without new lesions developing. C
Avoid body contact until after treatment and follow-up of patient and partner(s).
Bedding and clothing should be decontaminated using the hot cycle, dry-cleaned, or removed from body contact for at least 72 hours. Fumigation of living areas is unnecessary.
Keep fingernails closely trimmed to reduce injury from excessive scratching.
Immunocompromised or elderly institutionalized patients admitted with unrecognized crusted scabies are the main source of nosocomial transmission.

In institutional outbreaks, measures to prevent spread include quarantining and treating index cases, contact precautions with patient and fomites, and retesting cases 2 to 4 weeks after completing treatment.
Consider scabies in older adults with generalized or severe pruritus.
Permethrin 5% is the drug of choice for pregnant women.
Likewise, topical permethrin is the drug of choice for lactating women.
Topical lindane and oral ivermectin should generally be avoided during pregnancy.
Permethrin should be applied from head to toe.
In infants, it should be applied to the hairline, neck, scalp, temple, and forehead.
It has been shown to be safe in neonatal scabies, although the time of exposure was limited to less than 6 hours before washing off.
The safety of ivermectin in children who weigh less than 15 kg has not been determined.
